item.title: AI support agent in production
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Solo-built agent that researches every new support ticket for 200+ client organisations and delivers a diagnosis note in 1–2 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
Built end-to-end at a managed service provider, from the first design document to the production rollout. The agent sits in the support flow: every new ticket is picked up automatically, researched across the company’s tooling, and handed back to the engineer with a diagnosis note before they have opened it.
From idea to production took seven weeks. The agent now runs about 45 times per workday for 200+ client organisations. The first week saw 200+ runs and zero data incidents.Simplified architecture. Internal names, addressing and client details are left out on purpose.
How a run works
A new ticket arrives in the PSA. A small trigger job picks it up through a Service Bus queue and starts exactly one run for exactly one ticket. The request to the agent is signed, so nothing else can start a run.
The agent researches. It uses 17 read-only tools over Autotask (tickets and history), IT Glue (documentation) and Datto RMM (endpoints), exposed through an MCP server. The server fixes the ticket and the client scope for the run before the model starts; the model cannot widen it.
The model reasons over what the tools return. Model calls leave the network through a NAT gateway with a fixed outbound address.
One write, nothing else. The result is a diagnosis note with a proposed next step, written as an internal note on the ticket. That is the only write path the agent has. The engineer reads it and decides.
Every run is stored in PostgreSQL with its inputs, tool calls and output, so each note can be traced back.
Platform as code
The whole platform is defined in Bicep and deployed from the pipeline, nothing by hand:
Azure Container Apps for the agent, the MCP server and the trigger job, each with its own managed identity and scale-to-zero when idle.
Service Bus queue between ticket intake and the agent.
PostgreSQL Flexible Server with Entra authentication only, no passwords.
Key Vault for every token and signing key, read at runtime through managed identity with access granted per secret.
Container Registry with the admin user disabled; images are pulled by digest.
Private virtual network: data services are reachable through private endpoints only, public access is switched off, and all outbound traffic leaves through the NAT gateway.
Log Analytics collects application logs, Key Vault audit events and database metrics, with alert rules on top.
Delivery pipeline
Azure DevOps runs the whole chain on every pull request: unit tests,pip-audit for vulnerable dependencies,gitleaks for leaked secrets, an image build pushed through workload identity federation (no stored registry credentials), and a health-checked rollout. A branch policy onmain requires green tests, so nothing reaches production untested or unscanned.
Security by design
The rule throughout: the boundary lives in code, never in a prompt.
One ticket per run. The scope is set by the server before the model starts and cannot be changed by the model.
Zero credentials inside the agent. The agent process has no tokens for client systems; only the MCP server talks to the APIs, and it reads its tokens from Key Vault at runtime.
Secret fields filtered. Password-type fields from documentation never reach the model; the agent gets the item name and a link, not the value.
Prompt injection detected and refused. Ticket text is untrusted input. Instructions hidden in a ticket or an attachment are recognised and the run refuses to act on them.
Read-only by construction. The tools are read-only and the single write is the internal note. Execution of proposals is a separate, later component with its own identity and its own vault.
What’s next
A second agent for sales is in design. It gets an MCP server as its only write path and a human approval step before any message is sent. The execution side of the support agent follows the same pattern: fixed building blocks, approved by an engineer in the ticket, carried out by a separate service that checks the approval itself. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments API
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Spring Boot payments service with PostgreSQL and Flyway, on its way to Kubernetes with a scanned CI/CD pipeline.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
A small payments service built to practice platform work at a payments-grade standard: strict business rules, migrations, tests, and a delivery pipeline that scans before it ships.
What exists today
Spring Boot service with an accounts and transfers API, including balance checks and business-rule exceptions.
PostgreSQL schema managed by Flyway migrations.
A unit test for the transfer rules and an integration test for the full transfer flow, run through the Maven wrapper.
Next
Docker multi-stage build.
Kubernetes manifests, first on the homelab cluster.
GitHub Actions pipeline with Trivy image scanning.
AKS via Terraform.
Prometheus metrics and a Grafana dashboard. ]]>

item.title: Monitoring Homelab
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Production-style Prometheus, Grafana and Alertmanager stack on a 3-node Proxmox cluster, paging through PagerDuty.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
A full monitoring and alerting pipeline on my 3-node Proxmox VE cluster. Every config file was written by hand, no helper scripts or one-click installers, so that I understand what each line does.Data flow from exporters to my phone.
What’s running
node_exporter on each Proxmox host, exposing CPU, memory, disk and network metrics.
Prometheus scraping every target every 15 seconds and evaluating the alert rules.
Grafana with a custom cluster-overview dashboard.
Alertmanager grouping alerts and routing them to PagerDuty.
blackbox_exporter probing the HTTP endpoints of the services I run.
Everything except node_exporter runs together in one LXC container; node_exporter runs directly on each host because it needs the host’s kernel data.
Alert rules
Seven rules, each with afor duration chosen so a short spike does not page me.
AlertFires whenForSeverity
NodeDownnode_exporter unreachable1 mincritical
DiskSpaceWarningroot partition above 85%5 minwarning
DiskSpaceCriticalroot partition above 95%2 mincritical
HighMemoryUsageRAM above 90%5 minwarning
HighCPUUsageCPU above 95%10 minwarning
EndpointDownHTTP probe fails2 mincritical
SlowResponseresponse slower than 5 s5 minwarningAll seven rules loaded and quiet.
DashboardsCustom cluster-overview dashboard in Grafana.
Paging
Alertmanager sends firing alerts to PagerDuty through the Events API. PagerDuty opens an incident and sends a text message; if I do not acknowledge it, it calls. From crash to phone buzz is about three minutes for most alerts: thefor duration plus Alertmanager’s grouping window.
I chose PagerDuty over Telegram or Discord because it is what companies use, and I wanted to set up real incident management: escalation policies, acknowledgements, on-call.A resolved test incident in PagerDuty.
The cluster underneath
Three second-hand small-form-factor PCs (Dell OptiPlex, HP ProDesk) running Proxmox VE 9 as a cluster with high availability enabled. Storage is local on each node, with a 931 GB ZFS pool onpve for backups. Without shared storage an HA failover copies the container disk to another node, which takes minutes rather than seconds; fine for a homelab. All nodes are connected over Tailscale, with no ports exposed to the internet.The three nodes and what runs where.
What I learned
How Prometheus works under the hood: the pull model, scrape jobs, relabelling and PromQL.
Why Alertmanager is a separate component: grouping, routing and silencing are their own problem.
How companies handle incidents with PagerDuty: on-call, escalation and acknowledgement.
The install was the easy part. Understanding what each metric means, choosing thresholds that do not cry wolf, and building dashboards that actually help took most of the time. ]]>

item.title: Linux Security Hardening
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Two Bash scripts that bring a fresh Ubuntu/Debian server to a sensible baseline and audit the result.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
Two short Bash scripts: one hardens a freshly installed Ubuntu or Debian server, the other reports on the result. Tested on Ubuntu LTS.
Whatharden-server.sh does
Updates the system and enablesunattended-upgrades for automatic security patches.
Hardens SSH: no root login, no password authentication, port moved to 2222.
Configures UFW: default deny incoming, allow outgoing, open only 2222, 80 and 443.
Installs and enablesauditd for security event logging.
WhatSecurity-audit.sh reports
The active SSH settings forPort,PermitRootLogin andPasswordAuthentication.
UFW status and rules.
Failed SSH login attempts fromauth.log.
Packages with pending updates.
Audit output
sudo ./Security-audit.shLinux Security Audit SSH configuration:✓ Port 2222✓ PermitRootLogin no✓ PasswordAuthentication no UFW firewall status: Status: active Logging: on (low) Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), deny (routed) To Action From -- ------ ---- 2222/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere 80/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere 443/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere Failed SSH login attempts (last 24h): sshd[2376]: Failed password for project from 192.168.159.1 port 30414 ssh2 sshd[4581]: Failed password for project from 192.168.159.1 port 30543 ssh2 Audit Complete
Why
I wrote these to practice Linux administration and server-side security hands-on. The scripts are short and readable on purpose: every line is something I can explain and defend.
What I’d do next
For one server, Bash is fine. For ten, this becomes an Ansible playbook with an inventory, and the audit becomes a set of[OK]/[FAIL] checks with an exit code so it can run from cron or CI. ]]>
